title: Finite-depth scaling and an exact Bernoulli-leaf identity for the min-plus process on the binary tree
abstract: The min-plus process is a stochastic coagulation-annihilation-type process on the binary tree, of interest in mathematics, physics, and computer science as a tractable instance of max-type recursive distributional equations. We carry out large Monte Carlo simulations at effective tree depths up to $N=60$ that provide finite-depth corroboration of the Beta(2,1) stretched-exponential limit for its root value $X_{N}$ at $p=1/2$, on the asymmetric $\sqrt{N}$ side of the random-homogeneous-systems classification recently introduced by Chen, Duquesne, and Shi and by Morfe. Off criticality, our simulations confirm the sub-critical closed form $\mathbb{P}(X_{\infty}=1)=(1-2p)/(1-p)$ within Monte Carlo error and document a super-critical mean growth exceeding the elementary $(2p)^{N}$ lower bound at the depths we reach. For a Bernoulli($q$)-initial-condition variant, we identify an elementary closed-form identity at $p=1/2$ that pins down the order parameter $\mathbb{P}(X_{N}=0)=q$ exactly, locates the absorbing-state phase transition at $p_{c}=1/2$ in the operator-mixing probability rather than in the initial-zero density, and shows that the conditional law on positives deforms substantially with $q$. Our simulations use a level-wise recursion and an FFT-based precomputed leaf table which reduce the effective simulation depth while preserving the recursive tree law and may be useful for the simulation of related recursive equations on large trees.
summary: This paper investigates a stochastic min-plus process on a binary tree, analyzing its behavior across different parameter regimes defined by $p$. Using extensive Monte Carlo simulations and mathematical identities, the authors confirm that at criticality ($p=1/2$), the root value exhibits stretched-exponential scaling matching the Beta(2,1) distribution. The work provides both asymptotic theoretical results and precise finite-depth numerical confirmations for this complex random process.
main_problem: The study focuses on determining the asymptotic distribution of $X_N$, the root value, for a min-plus stochastic process defined recursively on a binary tree as the depth $N$ approaches infinity.
main_result: The paper corroborates that in the critical regime ($p=1/2$), the scaled logarithm of the root value follows a stretched-exponential limit characterized by the Beta(2,1) distribution. Furthermore, it derives an exact Bernoulli-leaf identity for specific initial conditions.
method: The research combines large Monte Carlo simulations (up to $N=60$) with rigorous mathematical analysis, including deriving closed-form solutions and performing extrapolation techniques on scaling laws.
model_or_system: The model is the min-plus stochastic process defined recursively on a rooted binary tree. The evolution at each node depends probabilistically on whether the parent value is determined by summation (probability $p$) or minimum (probability $1-p$).
key_observables: $X_N$ (root value), $\mathbb{E}[\log X_N]$, and the order parameter $P(X_N=0)$ for Bernoulli initial conditions.
important_parameters: The control parameter $p$, which defines three regimes: critical ($p=1/2$), sub-critical ($p<1/2$), and super-critical ($p>1/2$). The scaling rate is $\sqrt{N}$ in the critical case.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that finite-depth simulations can accurately corroborate established asymptotic theorems, particularly concerning the $	ext{Beta}(2,1)$ limit and the identification of universality classes for random homogeneous systems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the empirical distribution of $X_N$ confirming the Beta(2,1) profile at criticality, show scaling tests for $\mathbb{E}[\log X_N]$ vs. $\sqrt{N}$, and display the exact identity $P(X_N=0)=q$ for the Bernoulli variant.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model and analyzes off-critical regimes to find closed forms for sub-critical convergence. It then focuses heavily on the critical case ($p=1/2$), using simulations to confirm the $	ext{Beta}(2,1)$ scaling limit. Finally, it derives an exact identity for a Bernoulli variant, locating phase transitions in the operator-mixing probability.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum systems, the analysis of recursive random processes on tree structures and the identification of critical exponents ($\sqrt{N}$ scaling) are highly relevant to understanding entanglement structure or correlation decay in many quantum physical models (e.g., tensor network renormalization group flows).
